name: neon_2022
title: 2022 neon shock (Russia-Ukraine war: Ingas + Cryoin halt)
history_note: No major fab stoppages were attributed to neon; chipmakers had built stockpiles after the 2014 Crimea price spike (documented range: up to ~6 months at the largest producers, 4-6 weeks at smaller ones — the yaml's 6.0 is the documented upper end, see sources). Alternative purification capacity ramped over roughly 12-18 months (Korea: POSCO/TEMC line from Jan 2022, SK hynix 40% locally sourced by Oct 2022; China's share rose). Neon prices spiked ~9x invasion-day levels within ~6 weeks (China wholesale).

sources.publisher: Reuters (wire text via Business Standard mirror)
sources.supports: Ingas + Cryoin = 45-54% of world semiconductor-grade neon; both halted by 2022-03-11; 2014 Crimea spike ~600%; stockpile estimates 'vary widely'

sources.publisher: U.S. International Trade Commission (Executive Briefings on Trade)
sources.supports: Ukraine ~half of world neon (Soviet steel-industry legacy; byproduct of liquid-oxygen generation); Cryoin + Ingas unable to produce as of 2022-03-11; post-2014 prices spiked >600%; firms stockpiled
larger chip producers held up to ~6 months of neon; smaller makers 4-6 weeks; contingency plans date to Crimea 2014
China wholesale industrial neon ~9x the Feb 24 quote within ~6 weeks; China's global share projected to rise ~30% -> ~50%
40% of SK hynix neon locally sourced by Oct 2022 (POSCO), 100% targeted 2024 — the alternative-supply ramp
POSCO/TEMC neon line: 22,000 Nm3/yr from Jan 2022 (~16% of Korean demand)

value_notes: capacity_lost 0.5 sits inside the sourced 45-54% band. buffers.Ne_purified 6.0 is the documented UPPER end (largest producers only; smaller makers held 4-6 weeks) — kept as frozen since this event trained ALPHA; a data PR revisiting it must register predictions first (AGENTS.md rule 3).
band_note: The band is a round-number encoding of the qualitative record above, written before statuses were computed; it is not a measured statistic. With a ~0% dip the 95%-recovery metric degenerates to time-of-minimum, hence the wide recovery band.

name: tohoku_2011
title: 2011 Tohoku earthquake (advanced wafer supply)

sources.supports: 25% of global silicon wafer production suspended: Shin-Etsu Shirakawa 20% + MEMC Utsunomiya 5%
Shirakawa production capacity recovered to pre-quake level by 2011-07-01 (partial restart 2011-04-20; inventory shipments from 2011-04-11) — ramp_tau_months 4.0 matches this ~3.5-month restoration
2011 worldwide semiconductor sales a record $299.5B, +0.4% YoY despite the quake — 'minor global impact'
TSMC held 'at least 30 days' of raw wafer/materials inventory

value_notes: capacity_lost 0.25 is the sourced IHS iSuppli figure (production suspended, not destroyed). buffers.Wafers 2.0 is ABOVE the best-documented figures (TSMC ~30 days; a Merrill Lynch analyst said 'mere weeks' industry-wide) — discrepancy recorded here rather than silently changed; a data PR lowering it must register predictions before the replay runs (AGENTS.md rule 3).
band_note: Round-number encoding of "minor global impact", written before statuses were computed; not a measured statistic.

name: sumitomo_1993
title: 1993 Sumitomo Chemical epoxy-resin plant explosion (chip packaging)
history: price spike, brief pain, no catastrophe

sources.publisher: Roanoke Times & World-News (Virginia Tech news archive)
sources.supports: July 4 fire destroyed the Sumitomo Chemical plant in Niihama supplying 60% of the epoxy resin for DRAM manufacture; some memory prices ~doubled in weeks (1MB module $55 -> $120); analysts called the rise anticipatory, 'not because [a shortage] exists'

explosion cut off 60% of world production of the encapsulation epoxy; most companies held one-two months of resin inventory (buffers 1.5 sits in this band); within a month Sumitomo had arranged >half its usual output from other Japanese producers
headline: memory-chip prices stabilize after the factory fire sent them soaring (fetch-blocked at citation time; verified live for the essay in blog PR #6)

value_notes: capacity_lost 0.60 is the contemporaneously sourced world-supply share. The 'brief pain' record: substitution covered >50% of lost output within a month, and the November 1993 UPI follow-up ('resin shortage averted', 1993-11-30) closes the arc at ~5 months — consistent with the acceptance band's recovery 3±3 mo.
band_note: Round-number encoding of "price spike, brief pain, no catastrophe", written before statuses were computed; not a measured statistic. Note the band floor is 0% dip: history records real pain, so a model that shows nothing at all misses too.
xfail_reason: The model misses this event twice, in opposite directions. Protocol v0 (imposed-tau, observing fab flow) shows dip ~0%: packaging halts do not stop fabs, so through the fab observable the event is invisible — the wrong-observable failure from the design history. Protocol v1 (adaptive, observing delivered flow) shows a ~58% dip with no recovery inside the 72-month horizon — a hysteresis trap: the adaptation law rebuilds capacity, but the price-mediated demand reallocation that pulled the real system back in months does not exist in the model. This is the failing test that motivates the demand/allocation work (PLAN.md §5) and opened the packaging_resin oracle (map/_oracles/packaging_resin.yaml).

name: photoresist_2019
title: 2019 Japan-Korea photoresist export curbs (analog replay)

sources.publisher: USITC (Office of Industries Working Paper ID-19-062)
sources.supports: July 1, 2019: Japan restricted exports of hydrogen fluoride, fluorinated polyimides, and photoresist to Korea; Japan ~90% of global photoresist production and >90% of Korea's 2018 photoresist imports; resist stockpiles typically minimal (shelf life 3-6 months)
Korean chipmakers held about two months of inventories (company-dependent) — buffers 2.0
first individual license (EUV photoresist to Samsung) approved 2019-08-08 — the fast-license ramp behind ramp_tau_months 1.0
photoresist exports permitted from August; moved to a bulk general license in December 2019 — realized photoresist disruption small
hydrogen fluoride exports to Korea fell ~87.9%, but NOT photoresist or fluorinated polyimide — the non-event applies to the photoresist channel this replay models

value_notes: feared_capacity_lost 0.90 is the sourced Japanese share; capacity_lost 0.15 (realized) remains a session estimate of the small realized disruption — no source quantifies the realized photoresist supply drop directly (Korean chip OUTPUT showed no significant change, and licenses flowed from August). Nuance recorded: hydrogen fluoride, not modeled here, was the harder-hit material.
band_note: Round-number encoding of "non-event", written before statuses were computed; not a measured statistic. The adaptive protocol scores the realized (~15%) replay; the feared (90%) adaptive replay is an unscored counterfactual.

name: chip_crunch_2021
title: 2020-21 chip crunch (demand-side)
history: demand surge + ordering whiplash while fab capacity stayed intact; shortages persisted ~2 years

sources.supports: demand surge + just-in-time auto supply chains more to blame than pandemic supply disruption; automakers canceled chip contracts then could not reorder (bullwhip), locked out from early 2021 to mid-2022
shortage hobbled vehicle production for most of 2021 and 2022; 'new normal' by mid-2023 — the ~2-year duration
TSMC running at 'over 100% utilization' — fab capacity intact and saturated, i.e. a demand-side event
